content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
Summary
-------------
This paper first measures sentiment bias in language models as reflected by text generated by the models. The models are conditioned on prefix texts that have certain attributes (e.g., gender), and then generate continuations. Then a sentiment classifier is used to evaluate whether the generated text exhibits bias. The classifier are used for calculating certain fairness metrics. To reduce bias, the paper adds other objective terms to the usual language modeling objective, where the new term encourages similarity between two texts generated by conditioning on attributes from different groups. This similarity may be employed at either the language model hidden representations or after a projection in the sentiment classifier. The proposed new models show reduced bias according to the fairness measures, while obtaining similar perplexity to the baseline model and slightly reduced semantic similarity of the generated text to the conditioning context. 

The paper does a very good job of motivating and situating the work in light of recent research. The problem is important and timely. The adaptation of metrics from fair ML may be useful for other scenarios handling bias in NLP models. The proposed regularization techniques are interesting and may also be useful in other contexts. 
The experimental setup makes some assumptions that are not completely justified in my opinion. In particular: (1) using a sentiment classifier to assess bias may be problemantic; (2) the templates may lead to mostly neutral texts; (3) the semantic-similarity measure may not be very informative; Please see detailed remarks below.  

According to the ICLR call for papers, papers exceeding 8 pages will be held to a higher standard. At present, I think the paper needs to be improved to meet this expectation. I am willing to reconsider my evaluation depending on the author response.  


Main comments
----------------------
1. The sentiment in generated texts is assessed via a sentiment classifier. The authors acknowledge that the classifier "is not perfect and might exhibit some biases" and "leave investigation of an unbiased evaluator to future work". I think this is a reasonable approximation, but would like to propose at least a small-scale human evaluation of sentiment in the generated texts.
2. Besides the question of whether the classifier is biased, one concern that I have with the methodology is that most generated texts may not have a very strong sentiment signal in either direction. The templates and examples given in the paper and appendix suggest that most generated text might just be neutral in its sentiment. The histograms in figures 2+3 also hint at that. The fact that the histogram in figure 2 shows bias which is less evident in figure 3 is a good evidence to the issues discussed in the paper. However, if indeed most sentiment is neutral, the magnitude of bias might be quite small. I'm not sure how to interpret the magnitude of the various fairness metrics, but the numbers in tables 2+3 appear quite small. 
3. It makes sense to evaluate perplexity to judge the quality of the generated texts and the tradeoff with fairness. It is also important to evaluate whether the generated texts is faithfull/consistent with the prompt, which seems to be what the semantic similarity gets at. However I'm not sure it makes much sense to measure cosine similarity of a sentence representation and one word embedding. I am also not sure whether the semantic similarities are reasonable. The comment on how empirically irrelevant sentences happen when there is a >20% drop in semantic similarity is also made in passing. It may be good to re-consider how to measure semantic similarity, as well as provide more examples/statistics on what makes a large difference. In this context, a human evaluation may be very helpful. 

Other comments
-----------------------
1. The related work is comprehensive and sets the background well for the paper problem setup and contributions. 
2. The point made about specifying the fairness measure based on the distributions distance, rather than individual predictions, seems quite important. It does make sense to me. However, the proposed bias reduction methods then operate at an instance level, rather than the distribution level. Would it make sense to consider alternatives that work at the global level, such as posterior regularization?  
3. Does the methodology extend to multiple attribute groups? That is, a sentence may have more than one kind of attribute, such as both gender and race. 
4. What is P^*_S? Is this the sentiment score distribution over the union of all subgroups a \in A? Or something else? 
5. What are \alpha's in section 4, bottom of page 5? Also, the features end up being the average of the top two layers, based on the intuition that sentiment is a high-level property that should be represented at the top layers. This seems reasonable, but have you tried other layers as well? 
6. The concern of over-regularizing with the embedding similarity sounds plausible. However, giving a weight \lambda to the fairness objective, as is done, should be able to control that. I'm not sure this is a good motivation for the sentiment similarity, as that too may lead to over-regularization. In this context, do you back-prop through the sentiment classifier into the language model? 
7. The details on the sentiment similarity regularization are a bit blurry. Is it the sentiment score that is used or the projection? What projection exactly is used? I assume this is something from the 3-layered MLP mentioned later.
8. What are the baseline models w.r.t to the proposed regularized models? Given the curriculum training, it sounds like the regularized models are in fact the baseline models that are continuing to be trained with the regularization terms. This means that they were trained for longer than the baseline models, which may make the results less comparable (although perplexity values are similar). 
9. Have you evaluated the importance of curriculum training? What happens if models are trained from scratch with the regularization? For example, one could perform embedding similarity or even get the sentiment score/projection from an off-the-shelf sentiment classifier for the sentiment similarity regularization. 
10. I am not convinced that "[t]he simple counting-based method .. is less prone to giving biased judgements". Is there any evidence or further argument for that? 
11. I do not understand this sentence from page 9: "When fairness scores are similar, sentiment-similarity regularization achieves better fairness scores." 
12. Section 5, last paragraph: looks like the words "in Wikitext-103" are missing, to explain that the bias in Wikitext-103 is smaller than WMT-19. 
13. Comparing tables 2 and 3 (end of section 5) is tricky, because both datasets and models change between them. Thus it isn't possible to disentangle the two.  
14. Table 4 with the examples is mentioned but not discussed at all. Do we learn something from it? 
15. Kirichenko and Mohammad's paper appears twice in the references. 
16. Appendix B, last sentence isn't clear: "We sample with template of 1.0."

content.title: Replies to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful comments.

Major comment 1: We agree with you that using a sentiment classifier is only a reasonable approximation. We are conducting human evaluations to address your comments on using sentiment classifiers and the measurement of semantic similarity. We will include these results in the final version of our paper.

Major comment 2: In a concurrent work https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01326, the authors also similarly found that when generating a set of sentences, a lot of them have neutral sentiment scores. However, the language model could still possibly generate very biased and sometimes insulting sentences.  Figure 1 also suggests that commonly generated sentences are neutral in sentiment but there is a large deviation between distributions. Thus, the bias in language model must be evaluated distributionally using a large number of samples. This is why we propose novel fairness metrics to quantify the bias in a distributional manner.

Since the metrics are evaluated based on a sample distribution, we agree with you that it can be hard to interpret its magnitude (you can think of it as a “KL divergence”-like score, which is probably not straightforward to perceive at first glance), and we focus on the relative improvement of these fairness metrics. In Figure 1 (page 4 left), the group fairness score of the model is 0.327, and the score of model in Figure 2 (page 4 right) is 0.144. Hopefully these numbers help you get more intuitions behind the scores.

Major comment 3: measuring semantic relevance reliably is still an open challenge and the use of universal sentence encoder is only a proxy. We use the universal sentence encoder to encode both sensitive attributes and the generated sentences. In the universal sentence encoder paper (Cer et al., 2018), the authors show it can be used to encode both sentences and words and achieves strong results for several downstream tasks. We will add a human evaluation as a complementary study and add more qualitative examples in addition to Table 8. 

We hope the reviewer can re-evaluate our paper based on our response. Especially, if human study is the main concern, we will certainly conduct a small-scale human study and include it in our paper, but the main contribution of our paper will stay unchanged. 

Below we provide answers to other minor questions.

Other comments:
2. This is an interesting suggestion but it is challenging to consider global level when training large-scale language models. We will leave this investigation to future work.
3. Yes, the proposed method can be extended to cross groups by considering cross-subgroups attributes.
4. Yes, it is the union of all subgroups in \A.
5. We’ve clarified the description for \alpha.
6. We show that the sentiment similarity based method are less prone to over-regularization as it only penalizes the "sentiment dimension" of the embedding, while the embedding similarity penalizes the entire embedding. In other words, it retains higher semantic relevance while reaching a similar level of fairness scores. It also retains better fairness results while maintaining a similar level of semantic relevance. We add a Figure in Appendix D to show the trade-off between semantic similarity score and fairness scores. In this figure you can clearly see the sentiment similarity based method achieves a better trade-off. Regarding the sentiment classifier, we fix the sentiment classifier and backprop through it to update the parameters of the language model. 
7. We’ve clarified it in the updated version.
8. Our baseline LM is the LM from the first step of the curriculum training. In step 3 of the curriculum training, we only train the model with 1/10 of the language model training steps in the first step using a small subset of the training data, also with a smaller learning rate. The baseline model does not change too much even if we add an extra 1/10 steps as the perplexity already remains flat during the end of the first step. 
9. For the sentiment based method, we have to do the curriculum training as we need to train a sentiment classifier from the hidden states of the language models. An off-the-shelf sentiment classifier usually takes discrete text input instead.
10. We’ve clarified it in the text. The counting based methods only consider opinion words and does not contain any sensitive attributes. The learning based sentiment classifier might be affected in the sensitive attributes, as shown from previous study in Kiritchenko and Mohammad 2018.
11. We’ve fixed the sentence.
12. We’ve fixed the sentence.
14. We’ve clarified this. The purpose is to provide some qualitative examples and show the differences when changing the sensitive attributes.
15. We’ve fixed the duplicated reference.
16. We fix the typo “template”.

content.title: Preliminary feedback to author response
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed response. This is my preliminary feedback, provided in light of your request for feedback before Nov 9 (which I assume is due to the ACL anonymity deadline). It might be modified later on based on a more careful review. At this stage, I tend to stick to my previous evaluation, but I would like to give the reviews and responses a more thorough consideration, which I may not be able to do by Nov 9. 

1. A human evaluation of the sentiment in generated texts will indeed be helpful. This isn't the only major comment, but it is an important one. There may be other ways to mitigating the limitations of using an automatic sentiment classifier, such as comparing results of several such classifiers or taking an aggregate vote or estimating variance across such classifiers. 
2. I am still concerned about the potentially predominant neutral sentiment of the generated texts. A similar concern has been raised by Reviewer 1. The author response seems to be that neural sentiment is a viable debiasing solution (also referring to findings from Sheng et al.). However, one may want to get an unbiased but sentimental text. Also, perhaps it would be useful to look at the tradeoff between sentiment intensity and fairness. (I may have missed such an analysis.)  
3. The semantic similarity measure is still problematic in my opinion. The authors point to Cer et al. who used the universal encoder to encoder both words and sentences, and got good downstream task results. This seems plausible. My concern is specifically with measuring cosine distance between a sentence representation and a single word representation. This requires further support, or perhaps there are alternative automatic measures. 
4. The new figure in appendix D about the tradeoff is useful. Thank you for adding this, and addressing my other comments.  
5. Minor: I noticed that figure 2 changed from the previous revision, as well as changes in PPL numbers in tables 2 and 3 (some of them substantial). Could you explain these changes?

replying_to: Replying to Preliminary feedback to author response

content.title: Replies to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Thanks for your prompt response for the feedback. 

Overall, automatic measurements for fair sentiment classifier and measuring semantic relevance are still ongoing research. Our proposed framework is the first step in this field and it could leverage the advances in those fields to provide better debiased models in the future.
 
1. Agreed with your points. However, as we already measure two quite distinct sentiment classifiers (one is commercial sentiment classifier, and the other key-word based), not sure whether adding other sentiment classifiers (usually trained on much smaller datasets, potentially biased) will address your concern. As studying the debiasing in sentiment classifiers is still ongoing research and this is the first work in reducing sentiment bias in language models, we think this could leave for future work. 

2. To reiterate, we do not dictate the fairness goals, which is task- and context-dependent, but rather we offer tools for debiasing according to various fairness specifications. One canonical example of such a specification is the one we choose in the paper. However, the method is intended to be more general-purposed. 
For example, if having similar sentiment intensity is desired, one could add another regularization term to penalize the difference between original sentiment intensity and the new sentiment intensity.

3. We agree with your point but measuring semantic similarity is still an open question. We could view encoding a word as encoding a short sentence. Hence, there are solid results in measuring sentence similarity using the universal sentence encoder. 
We also tried keyword based matching for semantic similarity. Even though the overall trends are similar, keyword based method has higher false negative (missing some semantic relevant ones such as “driver” with a sentence mentioning “bus”). Again, similar to your point 1, even if we have another measurement, one could still argue that it is still not enough to measure them reliably. 

5. Regarding figure 2, we previously show the results from the sentiment-based models with a smaller regularization parameter. We replace it with a larger regularization parameter model. 
Regarding PPL, there is a bug we found after submission that we were only measuring a subset of the test set for PPL. The updated version is using the whole test set.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposes to evaluate bias in pretrained language models by using a fixed sentiment system. The core of the idea is that if you generate with a given prefix from a language model the distribution of scores assigned by a sentiment system should be the same if the prefix is drawn for the same equivalence class (i.e. if the prefix includes different country names, or different occupations or person names). Several different prefix templates are tested and an objective is proposed for reducing this notion of bias (essentially applying transformations on unsupervised data corresponding to the equivalence classes that will be tested and then trying to match hidden states between transformed and untransformed instances). 

Overall, I have concerns about this paper on (a) methodological and (b) experimental grounds. 

Methodological: I can't understand the motivation behind the mixing of a generation system and a sentiment analysis system. While I recognize one could generate with an lm and then analyze its output with a sentiment system, why would one do this? This just doesn't correspond to any real usage of pretrained lm in nlp, or how any sentiment system would work. Pretrained lm are used to provide representations on human authored text and then processed for downstream tasks.  Why not just follow the methodology of Kiritchenko & Mohammad ( https://www.saifmohammad.com/WebDocs/EEC/ethics-StarSem-final_with_appendix.pdf ) and just compute difference in accuracy among templates where sentiment is known?

Experimental: It seems like you are using the same augmentations for the training routine that will be testing your system on. Isn't it obvious that if you train your model to have equivalence for the small wordlists you constructed at training and then test with them again later, you will get improvement? I could not confirm any practical train/test separation between how the test was constructed and your proposed solution.  Furthermore, a simple missing baseline is just applying the augmentations and training with the LM objective and not doing any hidden representation matching.

Overall I really like the direction of constructing equivalence sets and thinking about model behavior counterfactually but I feel this particular work has significant mythological and experimental flaws.

display_title: We believe our paper does not have significant flaws

content.title: We believe our paper does not have significant flaws
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your review and comments on our work.

Regarding methodology:

As language models become more powerful, there are increasing number of work using language models as generative models, in addition to extracting pretrained representations for downstream tasks. We believe that a biased language model has the potential to influence social norms and perpetuate connotations associated with particular social groups, and it is important that we develop methodology to stir model outputs away from echoing unfair social biases (e.g., sentiment bias). 

We agree with the reviewer that traditionally we only use the learned representations in language model for downstream tasks, but now thanks to the success of large-scale SOTA language models (GPT-2 by OpenAI, MegatronLM by NVIDIA, etc), the trend is changing. Since these language models can generate realistic sentences, investigating the social impact of language models become crucial (cf. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09203 by OpenAI which discussed many potential issues in generated texts as well as several existing applications using LMs). Concurrent work to investigate sentiment bias in natural language generators also includes https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01326 (EMNLP2019). So we believe that our work is methodologically sound and reflects the frontier of this field.


Regarding your comments on train/test separation:

Since we aim to protect a set of sensitive attributes (the “small wordlists” as you mentioned), we have to let the model know what exactly these attributes are. Generalization in our work should be understood in a different sense: our test templates (Tables 5, 6, 7 in appendix) are not used during training, yet the model still knows how to protect sensitive attributes when they appear in these unseen templates. Conversely, if not all sensitive attributes are available during training, the model cannot distinguish sensitive attributes with normal attributes at test time (analogously, it is similar to  testing with unseen labels for a classification problem, which can be really hard). Additionally, in many previous works on fairness (e.g., Bordia and Bowman 2019, Qian et al 2019), a predefined set of sensitive attributes are needed and used in both training/testing. We thus believe our experimental procedure is technically sound.

Thank you for suggesting this simple baseline and we are running it on our end. We will update the paper with these results shortly. One potential drawback for this augmentation baseline is that the future context after the perturbed word might not be valid (e.g., after changing a country word in a sentence, the following texts do not match with the perturbed country name in context). In our proposed approaches, we extract the hidden states directly after observing the sensitive attributes, and do not fit the language model with these perturbed sentences.

Based on our response, we believe our paper does not have any significant mythological and experimental flaws. We hope the reviewer can re-evaluate our paper accordingly. Thank you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper presents two methods to debias the neural language models trained from large datasets. Concretely, one method is based on semantic similarity, i.e. two sentences describing the same content but with different control variables should have similar representation. The other method is based on sentiment similarity, i.e. regularizing on the predicted sentiments for sentences constructed with different control variables. There is no doubt that debiasing LM is important. The proposed methods also seem to be straightforward. My major concern is whether the resulting sentiment distribution associated with the prompts are desired and the generalizability of the method to broader categories of bias.

Detailed comments:
- Since the fairness metrics are defined based on sentiment prediction, it's surprising to see from Table 2 that the semantic similarity-based method is more effective than the sentiment similarity-based one.

- From Fig 1, the distribution seems to become narrower, i.e. the predictions after debiasing seem to be more neural and less extreme. I'm not sure if this is what's desired for a debiasing method. 

- Other types of bias, which are beyond sentiment bias, exist in the language models too, e.g. the implicit association between general/race/nationality and properties. How to generalize the proposed method to other types of bias? 

- grammar: "we can measure the the distance via cosine similarity."

content.title: Replies to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We thank you for your thoughtful comments. We answer your three questions as follows:

1. “Whether the resulting sentiment distribution associated with the prompts are desired” and “Predictions after debiasing seem to be more neutral and less extreme”:

The point you raise about the desirability of the sentiment distributions associated with prompts is an important one. Rather than prescribing a particular model behavior as desirable, we see our method as a tool to shape the outputs of a language model. We define and measure the biases against the fairness metrics, instead of measuring the shape of the distribution. Based on the fairness metrics, it is true that a desired fair behavior is to have similar distributions under Wasserstein-1 distance (Eqs 4, 5) for the sensitive attributes, based on the commonly used demographic parity criteria in fairness literature. We also study the importance of semantic similarity to avoid models ignoring the sensitive attributes. 

A concurrent work by Sheng et al. (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01326.pdf) shows that extremely biased and sometimes insulting sentences can sometimes be produced by language models. Debiasing the generated texts towards neutral sentiment is indeed a valid solution in this case.

2. Generalizability of the method to broader categories of bias:

We agree that it is important that the proposed method generalizes to other types of bias. We focus on a type of bias that we can measure using the output of a current NLP system in this paper (i.e., sentiment). However, our method can extend to other types of classifier outputs besides sentiment. As we mentioned in Sections 4 and 6, the proposed framework is a general tool and the specification classifier can be changed to other categories (e.g., emotion, sarcasm, hate speech, fake news).

Additionally, we want to point out that there are no previous works on reducing sentiment bias in texts generated by language models. Some existing works on debiasing other NLP tasks including (Zhao et al. (2019); Basta et al. (2019)) also can only deal with a specific type of bias (e.g. gender bias in occupation). We believe the problem of generalizing fairness between gender/race/nationality and other properties is very challenging and beyond the reach of our work, as we are the first work studying sentiment bias and fairness in texts generated by SOTA large-scale language models.

3. Regarding Table 2:

For Table 2, you mentioned that “semantic similarity-based method is more effective than the sentiment similarity-based one”. It seems that you meant “embedding similarity” based method is more effective than “sentiment similarity” based method. For both methods, we can control the trade-off between semantic similarity score and fairness score using the regularization parameter $\lambda$. A larger lambda increase fairness at the cost of removing some context information from sensitive attributes, thus reducing the semantic similarity score. Since we report models over a very few lambda’s (10,100,1000), sometimes the ranking of the two methods is unclear. 

Typically, sentiment similarity based method has better fairness scores (I.F., G.F.) than embedding similarity based method when the semantic similarity score is similar, as sentiment similarity imposes weaker regularization to the model and keeps more context. We add a Figure in Appendix D to show the trade-off between semantic similarity score and fairness scores. In this figure you can clearly see the sentiment similarity based method achieves a better trade-off.

We hope the reviewer can re-evaluate our paper accordingly. Thank you.

content.title: Contribution - for Reviewers 1 and 3
content.comment: To clarify our contribution, in addition to proposing the debiasing framework and two different debiasing approaches, our contribution includes discovering sentiment biases in language models and proposing metrics to quantify those biases based on demographic parity from fairness literature. Our proposed approach is the first method to reduce sentiment biases in language models. The framework can be served as a general tool for debiasing according to various fairness specifications.
